aiSummary: Choctawhatchee Bay is firing on all cylinders this Wednesday, with an active speckled trout bite reported bay-wide, bull redfish in the mix, and tarpon cruising nearby beaches — but summer heat and a 37% storm chance after 1 PM make an early start non-negotiable. Water temps are sitting at 86°F under a full moon spring tide, so fish will be most active in the low-light hours around the 6:02 AM high tide before the heat settles in. Plan to be off the open water by early afternoon, and keep one eye on the western sky as convective storms can build quickly.

bridge.aiNote: The 331 Bridge spans the narrow neck of Choctawhatchee Bay, creating a current funnel where bait gets pushed through on both tides. Pilings hold speckled trout, redfish, sheepshead, and black drum year-round, with the lee-side pilings serving as the prime ambush zone on incoming tides. Because it sits on open water, it's the first spot on the bay to become unfishable when wind picks up or weather moves through.
bridge.todaysCall: The high tide crests right at sunrise (6:02 AM), which is about as good a setup as you can ask for at the bridge — hit the lee-side pilings immediately as the tide begins to ebb and bait starts funneling through the structure. The full moon spring tide means stronger-than-average current, so heavier jig heads or weighted rigs will help you stay in the strike zone. Light westerly winds of 5–10 mph are manageable this morning, but the open exposure here means conditions deteriorate fast if storms fire early — with a 37% chance after 1 PM, make the bridge your first stop and wrap up well before noon. Slightly stained water today actually works in your favor at the pilings, as trout and reds will be holding tighter to structure and are less likely to spook.

alaqua.aiNote: Alaqua Bayou offers protected water with a strong year-round redfish population, along with speckled trout and flounder at the mouth. The oyster bars at the creek mouth are the prime producing zone, and tree cover keeps the bayou a few degrees cooler than the open bay while offering shelter from wind and weather. The upper creek transitions to brackish water and can hold bass alongside smaller redfish.
alaqua.todaysCall: Alaqua's tree cover and protected layout make it a smart choice on a day threatening afternoon storms — you can fish comfortably into late morning without worrying much about wind or lightning exposure. Work the oyster bars at the creek mouth on the falling tide, which will be running through most of the morning and into the early afternoon toward the 5:01 PM low. The full moon spring tide will push a stronger-than-usual ebb through those bars, concentrating bait and giving ambush predators like reds and trout a natural feeding edge. Slightly stained water suits this spot well — use noisy topwaters or rattling lures early, then transition to soft plastics worked slowly along the oyster edges as the sun climbs and the bite shifts deeper.

basin.aiNote: Basin Bayou sees less fishing pressure than Alaqua and LaGrange, which tends to produce less-educated, more cooperative fish. The interior grass flats are classic sight-fishing territory for redfish in under two feet of water. Pompano occasionally show at the mouth on moving tides in late spring and early summer, and the bayou is less protected than LaGrange when weather builds.
basin.todaysCall: With the tide falling all morning toward a 5:01 PM low, the interior grass flats at Basin Bayou will be draining steadily — this is your window to intercept redfish pushed out of skinny water and stacking along the deeper flat edges. Get there early; at 86°F water temps, reds on the flats will go lethargic once the sun is fully up and heat index climbs toward 111°F. The slightly stained water limits sight-fishing visibility somewhat, so work the edges methodically with weedless soft plastics or gold spoons rather than relying on pure sight casting. Keep your storm exit plan in mind — Basin Bayou is less sheltered than LaGrange, so if clouds start building after 1 PM, don't linger.

lagrange.aiNote: LaGrange Bayou is the top trout producer in this area, with legendary oyster bars at the mouth and interior grass flats that hold redfish year-round. Deep holes inside the bayou hold black drum and sheepshead, and the surrounding geography makes it the most protected water on the north side of the bay when weather builds.
lagrange.todaysCall: LaGrange is the strongest all-around choice for today — the oyster bars at the mouth will be activated by a strong spring-tide ebb running from the 6:02 AM high toward the 5:01 PM low, and the bay-wide trout bite reported this week fits perfectly with this spot's well-documented production. Hit the mouth oyster bars at first light when tide movement is strongest and temperatures are still tolerable, working DOA shrimp or paddle-tail soft plastics along the edges. As the morning progresses and water drops, transition into the interior grass flats for redfish, then probe the deeper holes for black drum and sheepshead if the bite slows topside. The protected nature of LaGrange means you can fish here longer into the morning than exposed spots, though you should still plan to wrap up before the afternoon storm window opens after 1 PM.

fourmile.aiNote: Four Mile Creek is a tidal creek running between Shipyard Marina and the bay, where tidal flow pushes baitfish up the creek on incoming tides and concentrates redfish and trout in the bends and grass edges. The creek mouth is a prime flounder zone, and the upper section transitions toward brackish water with bass and smaller reds. It's the shortest and most protected fishery in this area when weather threatens.
fourmile.todaysCall: Four Mile Creek is your best insurance policy today — it's the safest spot on this dashboard when afternoon storms threaten, and its short, protected layout means you can fish it even if conditions deteriorate earlier than expected. The tide is falling all day from the 6:02 AM high, so focus on the creek bends and grass edges where bait gets pinned on the ebb; redfish and trout will stack in these ambush spots. Work the creek mouth carefully for flounder as the outgoing tide flushes shrimp and small baitfish past the structure — the full moon spring tide gives that flush extra push today. If you have a late start or want a lower-stress option given the heat index hitting 111°F, Four Mile's shade and protected water make it more forgiving than the open bay.

hogtown.aiNote: Hogtown Bayou is a signature Santa Rosa Beach guide spot and one of the most consistently productive trout flats on Choctawhatchee Bay. Summer mornings are the peak period, with speckled trout stacked on grass in two to four feet of water. Spanish mackerel show at the mouth on moving tides, and it's worth noting that Hogtown sits further from the 331 Bridge than the other bayous — factor in run time when planning your trip.
hogtown.todaysCall: The bay-wide trout bite reported this week maps directly onto Hogtown's signature pattern — trout on the grass flats in 2–4 feet — and a summer Wednesday morning with a full moon tide is about as good a setup as it gets here. Leave the ramp early enough to account for the run time and be on the flat by first light; trout will be most aggressive in the low-light window before the heat builds toward that 111°F heat index. The falling tide from the 6:02 AM high will move water across the grass and funnel bait toward the mouth, where Spanish mackerel may also be prowling — have a light wire leader and a fast-moving lure ready if you see surface activity. Get off the water well before the 1 PM storm window; Hogtown's distance from the ramp means you need to leave extra buffer time to make it back safely.

mallet.aiNote: Mallet Bayou is a small tributary that feeds directly into LaGrange Bayou, just south of Freeport. Its direct connection to LaGrange — the top trout producer on this side of the bay — means the oyster-bar trout-and-redfish pattern from LaGrange plausibly extends into this quieter, smaller water, though there is far less documented fishing history for Mallet Bayou itself. Its small, interior character makes it a likely calm-water fallback when wind picks up on the open bay.
mallet.todaysCall: Mallet Bayou pairs naturally with a LaGrange trip today — if the main bayou mouth gets crowded (a real possibility given summer charter pressure), sliding up into Mallet can put you on less-pressured fish that share the same habitat and feeding patterns. Work any oyster structure or grass edges you can find on the falling tide, using the same soft-plastic rigs that would be working in LaGrange proper. Don't expect the same documented productivity — this is a secondary move, not a primary destination — but the full moon spring-tide ebb pushing through the connected system could concentrate bait in the tighter water here. The small, interior character offers good storm shelter if afternoon buildups arrive earlier than the forecast 1 PM window.

mack.aiNote: Mack Bayou sits on the barrier-island (30-A) side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, well west of the 331 Bridge — it's a long-run destination, not a quick local trip. The bayou shares the same protected character as Alaqua and LaGrange, featuring marsh grass, oyster bars, and interior holes, and sees less fishing pressure simply due to its distance from the main boat ramps. Hewett Bayou and Buck Bayou sit immediately to the east and are realistically fishable in the same trip.
mack.todaysCall: Committing to the run to Mack Bayou today requires an especially early departure — you need to be on the water at or before sunrise given the afternoon storm window opening at 1 PM and the long run back to the ramp. The payoff is legitimately light-pressured water with the same oyster-and-grass habitat that's producing trout and redfish across the bay right now. Work the mouth structure on the falling tide with soft plastics or live shrimp, then probe interior holes as the morning progresses. Build a hard turnaround time into your plan — likely no later than 10–11 AM — to ensure you're back across open water well before afternoon storms can develop.

hewett.aiNote: Hewett Bayou sits immediately east of Mack Bayou on the barrier-island (30-A) side of Choctawhatchee Bay, near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park. It offers the same protected-bayou habitat as its neighbors, with oyster bars and marsh grass at the mouth and deeper interior holes further in. Light fishing pressure due to its distance from the main ramps makes it a worthwhile stop alongside Mack and Buck Bayou in the same trip.
hewett.todaysCall: Hewett is best approached as part of a coordinated 30-A bayou trip with Mack and Buck today — the run time investment is the same, so covering all three makes the long ride worthwhile. The falling tide running from early morning toward the 5:01 PM low will activate the oyster bars at the mouth; start there and work inward as water drops and fish reposition to the deeper interior holes. The full moon spring tide means more water movement than a typical day, which is a genuine advantage on these quieter, lower-flow bayous. Same hard time rule applies as for Mack — plan to be heading back well before 1 PM given the storm risk and the long open-water run.

buck.aiNote: Buck Bayou is the smallest and least-documented of the three neighboring bayous on the barrier-island (30-A) side of Choctawhatchee Bay, near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park. Its habitat should track its larger neighbors — marsh grass, some oyster structure, and a modest interior — but there is less basis to speak with confidence about its productivity. It's best treated as a bonus stop on a Mack and Hewett Bayou trip rather than a standalone destination.
buck.todaysCall: Buck Bayou is a low-commitment add-on to a Mack/Hewett trip today — if you're already out on the 30-A side and have time before your weather-driven turnaround, a quick pass through Buck's mouth structure on the falling tide costs you very little and could yield opportunistic reds or trout. Don't build your day around it; given limited documented history here, it's the last priority in the three-bayou rotation. The same time constraints apply regardless — the 1 PM storm window and the long open-water run home mean you should treat any time at Buck Bayou as a bonus, not a given. If the bite is hot at Mack or Hewett, stay there rather than moving for the sake of covering water.
